```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", out.width = "95%")
needed <- c("ggplot2", "rpart", "rpart.plot", "randomForest", "pROC",
            "knitr", "scales", "gridExtra")
missing <- needed[!vapply(needed, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing) > 0) {
  install.packages(missing, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
}
invisible(lapply(needed, library, character.only = TRUE))
set.seed(2026)

url <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IBM/",
              "employee-attrition-aif360/master/data/emp_attrition.csv")
d <- read.csv(url, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(d)[1] <- "Age"
constant_cols <- names(d)[vapply(d, function(x) {
  length(unique(x[!is.na(x)])) <= 1
}, logical(1))]
d <- d[, !(names(d) %in% c(constant_cols, "EmployeeNumber")), drop = FALSE]
d$Attrition <- factor(d$Attrition, levels = c("No", "Yes"))
character_cols <- vapply(d, is.character, logical(1))
d[character_cols] <- lapply(d[character_cols], factor)
```

## 1. The question and who needs the answer

**Which employees are more likely to leave—and what patterns can HR act on early?**

- **Audience:** Human-resources leaders planning supportive retention conversations.
- **Goal:** Identify patterns and compare models that can help prioritize review.
- **Guardrail:** Use predictions as decision support, never as an automatic employment decision.

*Presentation note: Introduce the business problem and explain that the analysis identifies associations, not causes.*

## 2. The data and what needed fixing

- **1,470 employees; 35 variables** in the source file.
- **237 left (16.1%); 1,233 stayed (83.9%).**
- The first column name needed repair (`Age`).
- Removed constant columns: `EmployeeCount`, `Over18`, `StandardHours`.
- Removed `EmployeeNumber`, an employee identifier.
- No missing values were found; no employee records were dropped.

*Why class balance matters: a model that always predicts “stayed” gets high accuracy but identifies no leavers.*

## 3. Two patterns that support the analysis

```{r eda-plots, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.5, out.width="100%"}
d$TenureBand <- cut(d$YearsAtCompany,
                    breaks = c(-1, 2, 5, 10, 20, Inf),
                    labels = c("0-2", "3-5", "6-10", "11-20", "20+"))

p_overtime <- ggplot(d, aes(x = OverTime, fill = Attrition)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("No" = "#56B4E9", "Yes" = "#E69F00")) +
  labs(title = "Attrition by overtime", x = "Works overtime",
       y = "Share within group", fill = "Attrition") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p_tenure <- ggplot(d, aes(x = TenureBand, fill = Attrition)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("No" = "#56B4E9", "Yes" = "#E69F00")) +
  labs(title = "Attrition by tenure", x = "Years at company",
       y = "Share within group", fill = "Attrition") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p_overtime, p_tenure, ncol = 2)
```

**What to point out:** Compare the *within-group* shares, not the raw bar heights. Overtime employees and employees in some early-tenure bands show a higher share leaving. These are associations, not proof of cause.

*Presentation note: Explain why proportions make comparisons fair when group sizes differ.*

## 4. The pruned tree: a rule HR can read

```{r make-split, include=FALSE}
yes_idx <- which(d$Attrition == "Yes")
no_idx <- which(d$Attrition == "No")
test_idx <- c(sample(yes_idx, floor(0.30 * length(yes_idx))),
               sample(no_idx, floor(0.30 * length(no_idx))))
train <- d[-test_idx, ]
test <- d[test_idx, ]
train$TenureBand <- NULL
test$TenureBand <- NULL

full_tree <- rpart(Attrition ~ ., data = train, method = "class",
                   control = rpart.control(cp = 0, minsplit = 20,
                                           minbucket = 10, xval = 10))
cp_table <- full_tree$cptable
min_row <- which.min(cp_table[, "xerror"])
eligible <- which(cp_table[, "xerror"] <=
                    cp_table[min_row, "xerror"] + cp_table[min_row, "xstd"])
chosen_cp <- cp_table[eligible[1], "CP"]
pruned_tree <- prune(full_tree, cp = chosen_cp)

# Choose the largest training leaf predicted as Yes for an example rule.
frame <- pruned_tree$frame
leaf_rows <- which(frame$var == "<leaf>" & frame$yval == 2)
if (length(leaf_rows) > 0) {
  selected_leaf <- as.integer(rownames(frame)[leaf_rows[which.max(frame$n[leaf_rows])]])
  path_list <- path.rpart(pruned_tree, nodes = selected_leaf)
  path_terms <- unlist(path_list, use.names = FALSE)
  path_terms <- path_terms[path_terms != "root"]
  rule_text <- if (length(path_terms)) paste(path_terms, collapse = " AND ") else
    "Follow the highlighted Yes-predicted leaf in the plotted tree."
} else {
  rule_text <- "This pruned tree has no leaf predicting Yes at the default class cutoff; use its probability scores and review the decision threshold."
}
```

```{r pruned-tree-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.2, out.width="100%"}
rpart.plot(pruned_tree, extra = 104, box.palette = "-RdBu",
           fallen.leaves = TRUE, main = "Pruned decision tree")
```

**Example positive-leaf rule from this fitted tree:** `r rule_text`

*How to read it aloud:* Start at the root, check each condition in order, and follow the matching branch to a leaf. The leaf gives the predicted class and the estimated share classified as leavers. The plotted tree is the source of the exact thresholds.

*Presentation note: Read the displayed rule in ordinary language; describe this as a risk flag for supportive review, not a verdict about an employee.*

## 5. Why prune the tree?

```{r tree-size, include=FALSE}
full_pred <- factor(ifelse(predict(full_tree, test, type = "prob")[, "Yes"] >= 0.50,
                           "Yes", "No"), levels = c("No", "Yes"))
pruned_prob <- predict(pruned_tree, test, type = "prob")[, "Yes"]
pruned_pred <- factor(ifelse(pruned_prob >= 0.50, "Yes", "No"),
                      levels = c("No", "Yes"))
full_test_error <- mean(full_pred != test$Attrition)
pruned_test_error <- mean(pruned_pred != test$Attrition)
```

- The **full tree** can keep splitting to fit details specific to its training sample.
- **Pruning** removes splits that add little cross-validated value.
- We used the **1-standard-error rule**: choose the simplest tree within one standard error of the minimum cross-validation error.
- The pruned tree has **`r sum(pruned_tree$frame$var == "<leaf>")` leaves**, versus **`r sum(full_tree$frame$var == "<leaf>")`** in the full tree.
- Test error: **full `r scales::percent(full_test_error, accuracy = 0.1)`; pruned `r scales::percent(pruned_test_error, accuracy = 0.1)`**.

*Presentation note: Training error tends to fall as a tree grows, but that does not guarantee better performance on unseen employees. Test error is a more useful check of generalization.*

## 6. Four-model ROC and comparison with guessing

```{r fit-other-models, include=FALSE}
# Bagging: average probabilities from bootstrap-grown trees.
bag_predictions <- matrix(0, nrow = nrow(test), ncol = 100)
for (b in seq_len(100)) {
  boot_idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(train)), nrow(train), replace = TRUE)
  bag_fit <- rpart(Attrition ~ ., data = train[boot_idx, ], method = "class",
                   control = rpart.control(cp = 0.01, minsplit = 20,
                                           minbucket = 10))
  bag_predictions[, b] <- predict(bag_fit, test, type = "prob")[, "Yes"]
}
bag_prob <- rowMeans(bag_predictions)
bag_pred <- factor(ifelse(bag_prob >= 0.50, "Yes", "No"), levels = c("No", "Yes"))

rf_fit <- randomForest(Attrition ~ ., data = train, ntree = 500,
                       mtry = floor(sqrt(ncol(train) - 1)))
rf_prob <- predict(rf_fit, test, type = "prob")[, "Yes"]
rf_pred <- predict(rf_fit, test, type = "response")

model_probs <- list("Full tree" = predict(full_tree, test, type = "prob")[, "Yes"],
                    "Pruned tree" = pruned_prob,
                    "Bagging" = bag_prob,
                    "Random forest" = rf_prob)
model_preds <- list("Full tree" = full_pred,
                    "Pruned tree" = pruned_pred,
                    "Bagging" = bag_pred,
                    "Random forest" = rf_pred)

make_metrics <- function(model_name, prob, pred) {
  cm <- table(Predicted = factor(pred, levels = c("No", "Yes")),
              Actual = factor(test$Attrition, levels = c("No", "Yes")))
  tp <- cm["Yes", "Yes"]; tn <- cm["No", "No"]
  fp <- cm["Yes", "No"]; fn <- cm["No", "Yes"]
  roc_obj <- pROC::roc(test$Attrition, prob, levels = c("No", "Yes"),
                       direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
  data.frame(Model = model_name,
             Accuracy = (tp + tn) / sum(cm),
             Sensitivity = if ((tp + fn) > 0) tp / (tp + fn) else NA_real_,
             Specificity = if ((tn + fp) > 0) tn / (tn + fp) else NA_real_,
             AUC = as.numeric(pROC::auc(roc_obj)))
}

comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(model_probs), function(nm) {
  make_metrics(nm, model_probs[[nm]], model_preds[[nm]])
}))
majority_accuracy <- max(prop.table(table(test$Attrition)))
comparison <- rbind(data.frame(Model = "Majority class (always No)",
                               Accuracy = majority_accuracy,
                               Sensitivity = 0,
                               Specificity = 1,
                               AUC = 0.5), comparison)
comparison_print <- comparison
comparison_print[, -1] <- lapply(comparison_print[, -1], function(x) round(x, 3))
```

```{r roc-and-table, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=4.5}
roc_colors <- c("#555555", "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73")
roc_list <- lapply(model_probs, function(prob) {
  pROC::roc(test$Attrition, prob, levels = c("No", "Yes"),
            direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
})
plot(roc_list[[1]], col = roc_colors[1], lwd = 2,
     main = "ROC curves on the held-out test set")
for (i in 2:length(roc_list)) {
  plot(roc_list[[i]], col = roc_colors[i], lwd = 2, add = TRUE)
}
legend("bottomright", legend = names(roc_list), col = roc_colors,
       lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

```{r comparison-table}
knitr::kable(comparison_print,
            caption = "Held-out test-set results at a 0.50 probability threshold")
```

**How to explain AUC:** It is the chance that a randomly selected leaver receives a higher risk score than a randomly selected employee who stayed. **0.50** is no better than ranking at random; higher is better.

The majority-class benchmark shows why accuracy alone is not enough: always predicting “No” can be correct most of the time while having zero sensitivity for leavers. Sensitivity and the cost of missed leavers should inform the final decision threshold.

*Presentation note: Compare the four ROC curves and table. Do not claim a meaningful winner when test results are close or based on one split.*

## 7. Recommendation: what we recommend and what we give up

**Recommendation:** Use the pruned tree as a transparent way to identify patterns for **voluntary, supportive HR follow-up**. Compare its results against bagging and random forest before selecting a model for further testing.

- We gain a short, explainable rule with the tree.
- We may give up some predictive performance compared with ensemble models.
- The test metrics come from one random split and need confirmation with repeated splits or cross-validation.
- Attrition predictors are associations, not proof of causes.
- Do not use the model to make automatic hiring, firing, promotion, or compensation decisions. Review fairness and privacy before any operational use.

**Questions to prepare for:** Why prune? What does AUC mean for two employees? How does the model compare with always predicting “stayed”? Which error is more costly to HR? Would the recommendation survive a different split?

*Presentation note: Each group member should be ready to explain the question, data cleaning, plots, tree, and the limitations—not only their own slide.*
